To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) HL adults are sensitive to the quantificational meaning of universal quantifier every, but (ii) they make q-spreading errors when the visual context is referentially salient, but not when it is not, and (iii) the q-spreading errors in HL adults can be attributed to the cognitive overload caused by attentional demands of the visual context.

heritage Russian–English bilingual adults make quantifier-spreader errors in their weaker, non-dominant, heritage language, and only when they are presented with a visually salient, overexhaustive, context.

heritage language speakers are more likely than monolingual speakers to make q-spreading errors in a sentence-picture verification task when the picture contains extra objects that match the quantifier in number.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether bilingualism has a positive or negative effect on the development and maintenance of linguistic abilities.
how bilingualism affects the interpretation of universal quantifier sentences and how it interacts with visual attention.
the question of how bilinguals integrate linguistic information with visual information and how this integration is affected by language proficiency.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present study provides a new perspective on the role of attention in the interpretation of quantifier sentences in bilinguals.
q-spreading is not a robust phenomenon for HL bilinguals, but that it may occur when the task is cognitively demanding.

q-spreading is an effect of cognitive overload caused by attentional demands of visual context and a weaker, heritage, linguistic system, and that this is the reason why it is more frequent in bilinguals than in monolinguals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
heritage language speakers are not monolinguals in disguise and that the bilingual language processing system has a different architecture.

heritage language speakers are able to process sentences containing quantifiers, but they are not as efficient in doing so as monolingual speakers, and this may be due to their weaker heritage language skills.
bilinguals are able to integrate multiple sources of information in their weaker, HL, and that this process may be cognitively demanding.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HL speakers’ q-spreading errors are qualitatively similar to those of L2 learners and that they are not a result of a weaker L2 proficiency.
q-spreading is a robust phenomenon across monolingual and bilingual speakers.
HL speakers’ performance in language comprehension is affected by the language in which they are tested.
